name: TRT / testosterone for jaw

lead: Some looksmaxxing users take testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), or discuss related androgens such as DHT, hoping for a more masculine jaw, midface and neck.

The chain is hormonal: testosterone acts on the androgen receptor and is converted in tissues to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), linked to facial and body hair growth, while testosterone is linked to musculoskeletal development, voice deepening and libido. Testosterone medication is approved for men with low natural testosterone, for masculinising therapy in transgender men and for some other uses. No study of testosterone for jaw or facial bone structure in appearance enhancement was found.

paras: In medical use it is prescribed after testing and monitored over time. Users in forums discuss it alongside training, body-fat reduction and facial hair as part of a broader masculinising routine. Muscle, skin and hair changes appear over months.

Reported effects include acne, oily skin, hair loss, breast enlargement in men, raised red blood cell count, worsened sleep apnoea, liver toxicity with some forms and suppression of sperm production. Testosterone is Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and prescription-only in the EU.

chain: Claimed facial bone and muscle change
angle.text: Users discuss testosterone therapy and related androgens as a route to a more masculine jaw, midface and neck. Testosterone therapy is established for low testosterone and masculinising treatment, but no study tests it for jaw structure.

lead: TRT or testosterone for jaw is a looksmaxxing idea that testosterone replacement therapy, or related androgens such as dihydrotestosterone (DHT), can make the face look more masculine: a wider, squarer jaw, a heavier brow, denser facial hair, leaner skin-over-bone definition and more muscle in the neck and shoulders that frames the face. Forum members who discuss it link hormone levels to jaw and bone development, and some post photo logs of their aesthetic changes after starting therapy.[1][2][3]

Testosterone medication is an established treatment for men with low or absent natural production, for masculinising hormone therapy in transgender men and for certain breast cancers. Clinical descriptions of masculinising therapy list facial changes among the effects of androgens: a more prominent brow, a wider and more deeply sculpted jaw, enlargement of the nasal tip, a more visible Adam's apple, facial hair growth, more muscle and a shift of fat away from the cheeks and lips. Those effects are described in people who start therapy after puberty with little prior androgen exposure.

Testosterone is converted in tissues to DHT by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase, and DHT is the androgen mainly linked to facial and body hair growth and, in people predisposed, to pattern hair loss. Medical sources also describe risks: acne, breast enlargement in men, raised red blood cell count and suppressed sperm production.[4] No published study has tested testosterone therapy specifically for jaw or facial bone structure in men with typical development.

paras: The idea draws on how androgens shape the male face at puberty. Rising testosterone is associated with growth of the jaw and brow, thickening of facial hair and growth of muscle, and posts in looksmaxxing communities treat hormone levels as a lever for those traits.[1][5] Testosterone medication comes as injections, gels, patches, oral, buccal, nasal and implant forms.

Discussion usually separates three things: clinical testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) prescribed for diagnosed deficiency, higher-dose non-prescribed androgen use that forum members call blasts or cycles, and DHT-related questions about hair. The terms overlap in threads, and a single post may compare a 'TRT' regimen with a larger non-medical one.[1][5]

Wikipedia's account of DHT describes testosterone as supporting musculoskeletal development, voice deepening, sebum production and libido, while DHT, made locally from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase, drives facial, body and pubic hair growth. Circulating DHT is described as roughly a tenth of the level of testosterone, and DHT acts mainly inside the tissues that make it.

The same article describes people with 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency, a rare genetic condition with DHT around 30 percent of normal. They typically virilise partially at puberty, with voice deepening and musculoskeletal development, but have reduced facial and body hair. This is the usual reference point for the separate roles of the two hormones in hair versus skeletal and muscular change.

In the transgender medicine literature summarised on Wikipedia, males are described as having heavier bony brows, a wider and more deeply sculpted jaw and a more visible larynx, and androgen therapy is said to produce a more prominent brow, a broader jaw and growth of the nasal bone tips, while shifting fat away from the cheeks and lips. The article classes facial and body hair growth and voice deepening as irreversible, with the amount and pattern of hair largely set by genetics.

Some of the most active forum discussions concern teenagers and bone growth. A looksmax.org thread from a user who says he is 16 asks whether higher androgen exposure would close growth plates faster, and replies show members trading anecdotes about bone development under hormone use.[1] Another thread asks whether testosterone would help normal development at 15 for a person with a chronic illness,[6] and a before-and-after log is posted by a user who says he is 17.[3] These posts are personal accounts rather than clinical records.

Wikipedia's article on masculinising therapy notes that starting androgens before puberty is complete can bring a growth spurt followed by growth plate closure. Clinical guidance cited on this page addresses adult men with confirmed deficiency rather than adolescents seeking appearance change.[7]

Reviews of testosterone replacement describe goals of improving libido, mood, muscle and bone mass and anaemia in men with deficiency.[8] European guidelines for functional hypogonadism stress diagnosing it from repeated low morning testosterone plus symptoms, and note lifestyle change and weight loss as first approaches in overweight men.[7] Wikipedia notes that benefit for age-related low testosterone is described as unclear, and that a 2020 American College of Physicians guideline supports discussing treatment for men with sexual dysfunction and reassessing yearly.

In transgender men, androgen therapy is described as producing more prominent brows, a broader jaw, nose-tip enlargement, facial and body hair, deeper voice and greater muscle. The reference notes that cheek and lip changes come from fat redistribution rather than bone, and that facial changes develop gradually over time.

Wikipedia's article on anabolic steroids estimates that 1 to 3 million people in the United States use anabolic-androgenic steroids non-medically, and cites a survey in which most were non-competitive bodybuilders or non-athletes, many using them for cosmetic reasons; injection is the most common route. Looksmaxxing forums fall within this broader physique-enhancement culture, where members discuss androgens for muscularity, skin and facial presentation.[5]

The same article reports that in some surveys a majority of users had not told their doctor, and that where these drugs are controlled a black market supplies smuggled, counterfeit or clandestinely made products.

Hair loss is the best-documented appearance trade-off in forum discussion. Members ask how to pair androgens with DHT blockers and aromatase inhibitors in order to protect scalp hair while building muscle.[2] Wikipedia's DHT article says DHT contributes to pattern hair loss and temporal recession, and that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride and dutasteride lower circulating DHT by roughly 65 to 98 percent, with reported sexual side effects in about 3.4 to 15.8 percent of men and gynecomastia in about 1.2 to 3.5 percent.

Acne and oily skin are listed among the common effects of testosterone medication. Wikipedia's masculinising-therapy article notes that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors may reduce facial hair growth, which is why they are sometimes started after masculinisation is established.

Reported effects of testosterone medication include acne, oily skin, scalp hair loss in the predisposed, breast enlargement in men, mood changes, raised haematocrit and worsened sleep apnoea. Liver toxicity is associated with some oral forms. The anabolic steroid article additionally lists raised LDL and lowered HDL cholesterol, high blood pressure, enlarged left ventricle, testicular atrophy and mood effects among reported harms of non-medical use.

Exogenous androgens suppress gonadotropins and reduce testicular testosterone, which impairs sperm production; recovery after stopping is described as slow and variable.[4] A randomised trial in men with hypogonadism examined prostate safety events during testosterone therapy.[9]

Testosterone is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States, Schedule IV in Canada, Class C in the UK and prescription-only in the EU, and it is banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency. In February 2025 the FDA revised the boxed warning on testosterone products, removing cardiovascular outcome language and adding a blood pressure warning. Brand names for prescription products include AndroGel, Testim, Nebido, Xyosted and Depo-Testosterone.

No studies found on testosterone for jaw or facial bone structure in the context of appearance. Related research covers hypogonadism: reviews of testosterone preparations and their pharmacokinetics,[8] guidelines on diagnosis and monitoring,[7] a randomised trial of sexual function and hypogonadal symptoms,[10] and a trial of prostate safety events.[9] A 2025 review covers testosterone replacement and spermatogenesis.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, testosterone appears in threads about physique, bone development, hair loss and 'stacks', often alongside the abbreviations TRT and AI (aromatase inhibitor). Members debate hormone levels and facial outcomes in personal terms.[1][2][5]
